title: A homemade nightly script works around the missing export API
body: Because Pulse has no API, the participant wrote a script that downloads the CSV export every night and pushes it into BigQuery. He calls it *a bit of a hack* himself. A user investing engineering time to automate around the product is a strong signal of an unmet integration need. > "I even wrote a script that pulls the export every night, because there's no API for it." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]] ## Connections - contextualizes [[a-real-api-or-scheduled-export-is-the-top-time-saving]] - the workaround this request would replace

title: A real API or scheduled export is the top time-saving request
body: Asked what would save the most time, the participant answered without hesitation: a real API, or at minimum a scheduled export to a storage bucket. The lack of an API comes up twice in the interview (as the reason for the script and as the top request), making it the dominant theme for this technical user. > "A real API, clearly. Or at least a scheduled export to a bucket." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]]

title: After a wrong figure reached management, numbers are no longer trusted until cross-checked
body: A single incident, where the director asked about a gap she could not explain, changed the participant's behaviour: she now cross-checks every number herself before trusting it. This is stated explicitly and tied to a concrete event; it explains why the reporting is redone outside the tool. > "The director asked me where the gap came from and I had no answer. Since then, I don't trust the numbers until I've cross-checked them myself." > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]] ## Connections - extends [[pulse-numbers-do-not-always-match-the-carriers-data]] - the data mismatch is the trigger for the loss of trust - explains [[the-weekly-management-report-is-rebuilt-by-hand-in-excel]] - cross-checking is done through the Excel rebuild

title: Connecting the TMS took three weeks during onboarding
body: The participant describes getting started as slow, with a concrete figure: three weeks to connect the company's TMS (transport management system). Integration is the main bottleneck to time-to-value at onboarding. > "It was slow. It took us three weeks to connect our TMS." > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]]

title: Dashboard access is what customers value most
body: According to the participant, access to the shared dashboards is exactly what Fretto's own customers like most, which makes the access cap a real loss. This is second-hand (his view of his customers' preferences) and stated once. > "It's a shame, that's exactly what they like the most." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]] ## Connections - contextualizes [[guest-accounts-billed-as-paying-users-limit-sharing-with]] - what the pricing limit costs

title: Dashboards are perceived as clear once setup is done
body: Despite the slow onboarding, the participant judges the dashboards to be really clear once the integration works. Stated once, as a contrast to the setup pain: the product's interface is not where the friction lies. > "But once it was set up, the dashboards are really clear" > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]]

title: Data is exported to CSV and moved into the warehouse to combine with internal data
body: Pulse is used for visualisation, but whenever its data has to be combined with internal data, everything is exported to CSV and moved into the company's data warehouse. The participant describes this as something he does "a lot" and backs it with a concrete pipeline (BigQuery). This shows Pulse is not the analysis endpoint for data teams; the warehouse is. > "Pulse is good for visualizing, but as soon as we want to combine it with our internal data, I export everything to CSV and move it into our data warehouse." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]]

title: Guest accounts billed as paying users limit sharing with customers
body: Fretto shares dashboards with its customers through guest accounts, but each guest is billed as a paying user, so the company had to cap how many customers get access. The pricing model directly restricts the use case the participant identifies as most valued. > "We create guest accounts for them, but each guest counts as a paying user. We had to limit the number of customers who have access." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]]

title: Non-technical teams depend on support callbacks to complete setup
body: With no technical staff on the customer side, setup stalled until support called back. Stated once; it suggests (inference) that self-serve integration is not realistic for operations-led customers and that support availability sets the onboarding pace. > "Nobody on our side is technical, so we had to wait for support to call us back." > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]] ## Connections - explains [[connecting-the-tms-took-three-weeks-during-onboarding]] - waiting on support is part of why the connection took three weeks

title: Ops leads need to be able to explain every number to management
body: The participant does not ask for perfect data; she asks for enough context to justify the figures she presents. Inference: the underlying job is defending numbers in front of management, and the pain of having « no answer » for the director weighs more than the error itself. > "If I know the data is from last night, I can explain it." > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]] ## Connections - underlies [[users-want-to-see-where-each-number-comes-from-and-when-data]] - provenance matters because it makes numbers explainable

title: Per-user pricing charges for people who only view
body: The participant finds the price itself acceptable; her objection is to the per-user model, since about half of the users only consult the data. Stated once and clearly, in a single answer: the issue is the pricing structure, not the level. > "The price is fine. What bothers me is paying per user when half the people only look." > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]] She goes on to say that more view-only seats would be difficult to defend: > "If we had to add ten viewers, it would get hard to justify." > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]] Inference (low confidence): the per-user model caps account expansion to view-only stakeholders and could become a renewal or growth risk; she did not mention leaving the product. *Merged on 2026-11-04 with the note *Adding view-only users would be hard to justify at current pricing*, a second note drawn from the same answer.*

title: Pulse numbers do not always match the carrier's data
body: The participant states that Pulse figures diverge from the carrier's figures, with a concrete example: a delay rate shown as 4% that was actually 7%. A discrepancy of this size on a headline metric undermines the tool's value as a reporting source. > "Because the numbers in Pulse don't always match the carrier's. Last time, I presented a 4% delay rate when it was actually 7%." > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]]

title: Setup is expected to be harder for companies without a technical team
body: The participant speculates that setup would be harder for a company without a technical team. This is his assumption about other customers, not his own experience, hence low confidence; it is worth testing with non-technical customers. > "I understand it would be harder for a company without a technical team." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]] ## Connections - contextualizes [[teams-with-in-house-developers-set-up-the-integration-in-one]] - the flip side of the fast setup

title: Stakeholders without an account can only be shared screenshots by email
body: The participant wants to share a report with people who have no Pulse account. Because the CFO does not want a license, she emails him screenshots instead and calls this makeshift. This concrete workaround shows that the gap affects a senior stakeholder. > "Share a report with someone who doesn't have an account. Our CFO doesn't want a license, so I email him screenshots. It's a bit makeshift." > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]] ## Connections - related to [[per-user-pricing-charges-for-people-who-only-view]] - the CFO avoids a license, which ties sharing to the per-user model

title: Teams with in-house developers set up the integration in one afternoon
body: Setup at Fretto was very fast, taking a single afternoon, because the company has developers who connected the integration themselves. This shows that onboarding is smooth for technically equipped teams; the speed is attributed to their own capacity rather than to the product. > "Very fast for us, in one afternoon. We have devs, we connected the integration ourselves." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]]

title: The automated export depends on one analyst's personal login
body: The participant states that the script logs in with his own account to download the CSV. He did not raise this as a problem; the inference is that the pipeline is tied to one person's credentials, which points to an unspoken need for service accounts or token-based access for automated jobs. > "It logs in with my account, downloads the CSV and pushes it into BigQuery." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]] ## Connections - extends [[a-homemade-nightly-script-works-around-the-missing-export]] - how the workaround authenticates

title: The export script breaks whenever the interface changes
body: The nightly export script depends on the Pulse interface, so any UI change breaks it; this happened twice in the current quarter. Interface updates that look harmless to Pulse silently break customers' data pipelines, which (inference) can erode confidence in Pulse as a data source. > "When Pulse changes something in the interface, it breaks. That happened to me twice this quarter." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]] ## Connections - extends [[a-homemade-nightly-script-works-around-the-missing-export]] - the fragility of that workaround

title: The live delivery map is opened daily and replaces calling drivers
body: The live delivery map is the team's first screen every morning and has replaced phone calls to drivers to locate them. The participant mentions it unprompted (« my team loves the live delivery map ») and then confirms daily use, making it the clearest source of value in the interview. > "Every day. It's the first thing we open in the morning. It replaces calling the drivers to find out where they are." > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]]

title: The numbers are trusted as accurate
body: The participant, who cross-checks Pulse data in his own warehouse, says he has never seen a discrepancy in the numbers. Stated once, but from a well-placed observer. It suggests trust issues with Pulse lie in meaning and definitions rather than data accuracy. > "The numbers are right, on my side I've never seen a discrepancy." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]]

title: The weekly management report is rebuilt by hand in Excel every Monday
body: Pulse is meant to produce the weekly report for management, but the participant exports the data to CSV and rebuilds the whole report in Excel, which she says takes about two hours every Monday. This is a recurring, costly workaround that bypasses the product's core reporting job. > "In theory Pulse does that on its own. In practice, I export the data to CSV and redo everything in Excel. It takes me a good two hours every Monday." > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]] ## Connections - contextualized by [[after-a-wrong-figure-reached-management-numbers-are-no]] - the manual rebuild is driven by distrust of Pulse's numbers

title: Unclear metric definitions lead each team to interpret them its own way
body: Metric definitions are not documented anywhere, so teams interpret them differently. The participant gives a concrete example: whether a *delay* is measured against the promised slot or the estimated time. Inconsistent interpretations can lead teams to different conclusions from the same dashboard. > "But the definitions aren't clear. A "delay", is that relative to the promised slot or to the estimated time? It's not written anywhere. So each team interprets it its own way." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]] ## Connections - contextualizes [[the-numbers-are-trusted-as-accurate]] - the trust gap is about meaning, not accuracy

title: Users want a glossary of metrics inside the tool
body: Alongside the API, the participant asks for a glossary of metric definitions directly within Pulse. Stated once, as a secondary item in his time-saving answer. It directly addresses the inconsistent interpretation of metrics across teams. > "And a glossary of the metrics right inside the tool." > - Karim Benali, [[interview-karim-benali]] ## Connections - extends [[unclear-metric-definitions-lead-each-team-to-interpret-them]] - the requested fix for that problem

title: Users want to see where each number comes from and when data was last synced
body: Asked what would help, the participant asks for data provenance: a link to the source of each number or the date of the last sync. The request is stated once, in answer to a direct question, and is modest in scope - visibility rather than a new feature set. > "Honestly, seeing where each number comes from. Just a link to the source, or the date of the last sync." > - Claire Martin, [[interview-claire-martin]] ## Connections - addresses [[after-a-wrong-figure-reached-management-numbers-are-no]] - provenance is the proposed remedy for the loss of trust
